title: The ten, closed
hookLine: ten perfections, ten great lives, ten days of living them
tomorrow: can cutting mats or stocking shelves be practice?

lines: THE ONE YOUR WEEK ASKS FOR.
cards: Packing for a trip with one carry-on teaches you fast what you actually use. Today the perfections go into one bag, and the question is which one goes on top. Which do you need most right now?
The tradition's quiet answer: the one your week keeps asking for. A week of short tempers asks for patience. A week of putting things off asks for resolve.
A week of feeling invisible might ask for kindness, starting with yourself.

teach.b: Here are the ten, each with the great life that, tradition says, shows it. Generosity: Vessantara. Virtue: Bhuridatta, the naga prince who kept his precepts when captured.
Renunciation: Temiya, the silent prince. Wisdom: Mahosadha. Effort: Mahajanaka, swimming with no shore in sight.
Patience: Candakumara. Truth: Vidhura. Resolve: Nemi.
Kindness: Sama, kind even to the king who shot him. And equanimity: Narada, calm with a king who'd lost his way.

That's the Theravada list, set out in texts like the Buddhavamsa; Mahayana texts count the perfections their own way. Each one is a parami: a perfection, a quality brought to fullness. And look at the shape.

teach.h: BUILT ONE HARD SITUATION AT A TIME.
teach.b: Not ten trophies on a shelf, but ten strengths the Bodhisatta built across many lives, one hard situation at a time.
They lean on each other. Truth needs resolve. Kindness without wisdom can go soft; equanimity without kindness can go cold.
So you don't pick one and drop the rest. You pick the one that's next. And next doesn't have to be grand.
Patience with one coworker counts. Truth in one message counts.

how: In Theravada countries the great Jataka lives are painted on temple walls and retold at festivals and in sermons, and the ten perfections are taught as qualities lay people and monks can develop.

o: ten stages of meditation, in order
ten qualities built across many lives

games.q: each perfection, its great life — tap the pairs.
p: kindness, even to the king who shot him
equanimity, calm with a lost king
effort, swimming with no shore in sight

s: the ten perfections are ranked, with the best one last
they lean on each other; you pick the one that's next for you.
tradition ties each perfection to one of the Bodhisatta's great lives
Vessantara for generosity, Sama for kindness, Narada for equanimity, and the rest.
every Buddhist tradition lists the same ten
this is the Theravada list; Mahayana texts count the perfections their own way.

games.q: this week you snapped at your sister twice and at a cashier once. which perfection is next for you?
o: patience. the snapping is what this week keeps asking about.
generosity. it's first on the list, so you always start there.
equanimity. it's last on the list, so it must be the highest.
games.why: the list isn't a ladder. you pick the one your week is asking for, and the others lean on it.

practice: Hold up both hands. Touch one fingertip for each perfection as you say it under your breath: generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, effort, patience, truth, resolve, kindness, equanimity.
Go round once more, slower, and notice which finger you'd like to stay on.

wordCard.voice: The ten: the paramis, the perfections, from generosity to equanimity, each told through one of the Bodhisatta's great lives.

orig.note: Pali: parami, a perfection; the qualities the Bodhisatta fulfilled.

carryVoice: Your line: ten perfections, and one of them is next for you. Thirty of thirty, and the ten are closed.
